- **Gamekeeper** (3G) - 2/2 that can cheat out creatures when it dies
- **Far Wanderings** (2G) - Land ramp, potentially gets 3 lands with threshold
- **3 lands**: Island, Ash Barrens, Command Tower

This is a keepable hand. I have early mana fixing with Ash Barrens and Command Tower, plus the Island. Far Wanderings gives me ramp, and Gamekeeper is a decent early play. The big creatures are expensive but powerful for later. With Yidris as my commander, I want to be casting spells to cascade, and both big creatures synergize well with that plan.

Good start overall - let's keep it and play some Magic!

annotations.description: Casting Explore (a {1}{G} spell) on Turn 1 without having played a land first. Even if somehow they could cast it, the correct sequencing would be to play a land first, then cast spells. Explore draws a card and allows an additional land drop, so playing a land first (like Forest) would be essential to even have the mana to cast it. On Turn 1 with no lands in play, casting a 2-mana spell is impossible.

annotations.description: Cataclysmic Gearhulk's ETB trigger requires each player to choose one permanent of each type (artifact, creature, enchantment, planeswalker) to keep, sacrificing the rest. The Gearhulk is both an artifact AND a creature. By choosing it as the artifact to keep, the player still needs to choose a creature to keep — but since they're keeping the Gearhulk as their artifact choice, they could separately choose it as their creature too (a permanent can only be chosen for one category). Actually, a single permanent can only be chosen for one type. So by choosing Gearhulk as the artifact, they lose the ability to keep it as their creature, meaning they'd need another creature or lose their creature slot. More importantly, the Component Pouch is a pure mana-producing artifact with counters that provides ongoing value, while the Gearhulk is a 4/5 creature that would naturally be kept as the creature choice. By choosing Gearhulk as the artifact instead of Component Pouch, the player sacrifices their mana-producing artifact for no benefit — the Gearhulk should be kept as the creature, and Component Pouch should be kept as the artifact.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose Cataclysmic Gearhulk as the artifact to keep, which means Component Pouch gets sacrificed and the Gearhulk occupies the artifact slot instead of the creature slot.
annotations.betterLine: Choose Component Pouch as the artifact to keep, then choose Cataclysmic Gearhulk as the creature to keep. This preserves both permanents.

annotations.description: Cataclysmic Gearhulk's ETB trigger requires each player to choose one permanent of each type to keep and sacrifice the rest. The Gearhulk is a far superior creature - it's a 4/5 with vigilance that can attack and block effectively, while Wall of Omens is a 0/4 defender that can't attack at all. Since this is the creature choice for Gearhulk's ETB, keeping the Wall means sacrificing the Gearhulk itself, losing a powerful threat for a card that already drew its card on entry.

annotations.description: Consuming Aberration is cast before combat when Yidris (5/4) is on the board. Yidris has cascade on combat damage, so casting spells before attacking with Yidris means missing the opportunity to cascade into potentially better spells. Additionally, casting Consuming Aberration before playing a land means missing a potential land drop this turn - they have Mountain and Savage Lands in hand. The land should be played first to ensure no missed land drops, and spells should ideally be cast after combat to maximize Yidris cascade triggers.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Consuming Aberration (5 mana) before combat and before playing a land.
annotations.betterLine: Play Mountain (or Savage Lands) first to make the land drop, then go to combat and attack with Yidris to get cascade trigger, then cast Consuming Aberration post-combat (or cascade into something valuable first).

annotations.description: On turn 1, playing Savage Lands means it enters tapped and provides no mana this turn. Playing Mountain instead would provide an untapped red source, allowing potential use of 1 mana on turn 1 or guaranteeing untapped mana on turn 2. Savage Lands could be played on a later turn when the tempo loss of entering tapped matters less, or when you have other untapped lands to use. Without seeing the full hand, this is still generally suboptimal sequencing - you want to play tapped lands when you have no plays that turn only if you also lack untapped land alternatives, but here Mountain was available as an untapped option.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Savage Lands (enters tapped tri-land) on turn 1
annotations.betterLine: Play Mountain untapped on turn 1, save Savage Lands for a later turn when the tempo loss is less impactful

By playing it Turn 1 and cracking end of turn, you'd have an untapped basic for Turn 2 while preserving Swamp for a later turn when you need immediate mana. Playing Swamp first means Terramorphic Expanse will cost tempo on a later turn.

annotations.betterLine: Play Terramorphic Expanse, crack it at end of turn to fetch a Swamp (or other basic), having an untapped land for Turn 2

annotations.description: The reasoning references 'Guiltfeeder' which is not on the battlefield, suggesting confused card evaluation. More importantly, the reasoning doesn't mention attacking with Yidris, Maelstrom Wielder, which is critical here: with 0 cards in hand, Glint-Eye Nephilim connecting draws 4 cards, and if Yidris also connects, all those drawn cards gain cascade when cast. The Yidris + Glint-Eye combo is the most powerful line available. Not including Yidris in the attack plan wastes significant value.

annotations.betterLine: Attack with all creatures (25 total damage). Yidris connecting gives cascade to spells cast from hand, and Glint-Eye Nephilim connecting draws 4 cards to fuel those cascade casts. This is a devastating combo at 0 cards in hand.

annotations.description: On Turn 1, the player cast Kessig Cagebreakers which costs {4}{G} (5 mana), but this is Turn 1 where they should only have 1 land available. However, looking at the choices, they have land options (Forest, Tainted Wood, Terramorphic Expanse) available to play. Since it's Turn 1, they should be playing a land first, not casting a 5-mana creature. If they somehow have enough mana already (which seems unlikely on Turn 1), they should still play their land before casting spells to have mana available for future turns. The fact that Kessig Cagebreakers is listed as a castable option on Turn 1 suggests unusual circumstances, but the principle of playing lands before spells still applies - they should play a land first to avoid missing their land drop.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Kessig Cagebreakers before playing a land on Turn 1.
annotations.betterLine: Play a land first (Tainted Wood or Terramorphic Expanse for color fixing, or Forest), then cast Kessig Cagebreakers if mana permits. Playing the land ensures no missed land drop and maximizes available mana.

annotations.description: Blocking Nihiloor (3/5) with Guiltfeeder (0/4) means Guiltfeeder dies (taking 3 damage with only 4 toughness) while dealing 0 damage back to Nihiloor. Guiltfeeder is a valuable win condition that drains life based on cards in the opponent's graveyard via its Fear ability (nearly unblockable). The reasoning about 'Fear' is confused - Fear is an offensive evasion ability on Guiltfeeder, not relevant to blocking. Gamekeeper (2/2) would be a much better blocker here: it dies to Nihiloor's 3 power but triggers its death ability to reveal cards until finding a creature and put it onto the battlefield for free, providing card advantage and board development. Losing Guiltfeeder to block when Gamekeeper could block and generate value is a significant mistake.
annotations.actionTaken: Blocked Nihiloor (3/5) with Guiltfeeder (0/4), sacrificing a key win condition for no meaningful trade.
annotations.betterLine: Block with Gamekeeper (2/2) instead. Gamekeeper dies to Nihiloor's 3 power, triggering its death ability to exile itself and reveal cards from the library until hitting a creature, putting it directly onto the battlefield. This preserves Guiltfeeder as an evasive attacker while generating free board presence.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Blood Tyrant ({4}{U}{B}{R}) to add another 5/5 flying trampler that drains each opponent, or focus on combat first to see if Yidris can connect for near-lethal commander damage before spending mana on speculative flashback value

annotations.description: The player's reasoning is completely disconnected from reality - referencing Yidris cascade, Blood Tyrant damage, and combat resolving when none of these exist on the board. It's Turn 1 with 0 cards in hand, and the player is casting Horizon Chimera (which costs {2}{G}{U}) presumably from the command zone or some special zone. The alternative was activating Glint-Eye Nephilim. Without knowing the full game context, casting a 3/2 flyer with flash and life-gain-on-draw seems reasonable as a creature to put on board, but the reasoning is pure hallucination. However, examining the choice more carefully: if Glint-Eye Nephilim is already on the battlefield (it says 'activate'), then using its activated ability ({1}, Discard a card: +1/+1) requires discarding a card, and the player has 0 cards in hand, making that ability impossible to use meaningfully. So Horizon Chimera may actually be the only real option. Given the hand is empty, the activation of Glint-Eye Nephilim likely cannot be used (no cards to discard), making Horizon Chimera the correct choice by default despite the completely delusional reasoning.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Horizon Chimera
annotations.betterLine: Horizon Chimera was likely the correct choice since Glint-Eye Nephilim's activated ability requires discarding a card and the player has 0 cards in hand. The play itself appears fine despite the hallucinated reasoning.

annotations.betterLine: Play Terramorphic Expanse (or any available land) to develop mana on turn 1.

annotations.description: KimiK2 Sport chose not to block Nihiloor (a 3/5) despite having multiple creatures that could block it favorably. Nihiloor's combat damage isn't particularly threatening at 3 damage, but letting it through means Qwen3L Critic gains value from the attack (possibly triggering Nihiloor's 'attack with a creature an opponent owns' ability for life drain). With an 18/18 Consuming Aberration, 5/4 Yidris, and other creatures available, blocking Nihiloor with Guiltfeeder (0/4) would trade favorably - Guiltfeeder survives as a 0/4 blocking a 3/5 (takes 3 damage, lives with 1 toughness), and Nihiloor takes 0 damage. However, Guiltfeeder has fear and is primarily valuable as an attacker, and keeping all creatures untapped for a potential lethal counterattack next turn could be correct. The board state heavily favors KimiK2 Sport with massive threats, so taking 3 damage from 40 life is relatively inconsequential. This is borderline - not blocking is defensible given the dominant board position, but blocking with Guiltfeeder (which would survive and doesn't need to attack this turn) or Gamekeeper (which triggers a valuable death ability if it dies) could have been slightly better.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose not to block Nihiloor, taking 3 combat damage.
annotations.betterLine: Block Nihiloor with Guiltfeeder (0/4 survives blocking a 3/5 with 1 toughness remaining, preventing 3 damage) or Gamekeeper (2/2 dies to trigger its death ability, potentially putting a creature onto the battlefield for free).

annotations.description: On turn 1 with no cards in hand (likely just drew for turn with 1 card, but board shows hand=0 after playing), playing Reliquary Tower as the first land is suboptimal. Reliquary Tower only produces colorless mana and its 'no maximum hand size' ability is irrelevant early game. With colored lands available (Forest, Swamp, Jungle Hollow), playing a colored source first ensures you can cast spells on subsequent turns. Jungle Hollow entering tapped on turn 1 is essentially free since you likely can't cast anything anyway, and it provides colored mana plus 1 life.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Reliquary Tower as the turn 1 land drop, producing only colorless mana.
annotations.betterLine: Play Jungle Hollow (enters tapped but that's fine on turn 1, gains 1 life, and provides black or green mana for future turns) or a basic Forest/Swamp depending on hand composition for future draws.

annotations.description: KimiK2 Sport chose not to block any of the three attacking creatures (Nihiloor 3/5, Curator of Mysteries 4/4, Hama Pashar 2/3), taking 9 damage to go from 40 to 31 life. They have excellent blockers available: Consuming Aberration (25/25) could kill any attacker without dying, Yidris (5/4) could trade up or kill attackers, and even Guiltfeeder (0/4) could absorb damage. Most critically, letting Nihiloor connect means the opponent keeps control of any stolen creatures and Nihiloor's controller gains life/drains life from attacking with owned creatures. Blocking Nihiloor with Consuming Aberration would kill it cleanly (25 power vs 5 toughness), potentially freeing any stolen creatures and removing a dangerous engine. Taking 9 unnecessary damage while having a 25/25 that can block anything is a clear mistake.
annotations.actionTaken: Declined to assign any blockers, taking 9 damage (3+4+2) and allowing all attackers to connect.
annotations.betterLine: Block Nihiloor with Consuming Aberration (kills Nihiloor, Aberration survives easily) to remove the steal/drain engine. Optionally also block Curator of Mysteries with Horizon Chimera (both have flying, trades 3/2 for 4/4 but removes the flying threat) or block Hama Pashar with Gamekeeper (trades and triggers Gamekeeper's death ability to put a creature onto the battlefield for free).

annotations.description: Cast In Garruk's Wake before playing a land for the turn. With Forest and Swamp available as untapped land drops, playing one first would cost nothing and provide an additional mana source on future turns.

annotations.betterLine: Play Forest or Swamp first (free land drop), then cast In Garruk's Wake. This ensures no land drop is wasted and maximizes available mana on subsequent turns.

annotations.description: On turn 1 with no other lands in play, playing Jungle Hollow would have been better than Forest. Jungle Hollow enters tapped either way on turn 1 (when you likely have nothing to cast), gains 1 life, and produces both black and green mana. Playing Forest first wastes the opportunity to use turn 1's tempo-free window for the tapped land. Additionally, Rakdos Carnarium requires bouncing a land, so playing it turn 1 with no other land would just bounce itself — not viable. The correct sequencing is to play the tapped land (Jungle Hollow) on turn 1 when there's no mana needed, and save the untapped lands (Forest, Swamp) for later turns when you want to use mana immediately.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Forest as the turn 1 land drop.
annotations.betterLine: Play Jungle Hollow on turn 1 (enters tapped with no tempo cost, gains 1 life, fixes mana), then play untapped lands like Forest or Swamp on subsequent turns when mana is needed.

annotations.description: On Turn 1, casting Phantom Steed before playing a land is incorrect sequencing. Additionally, Phantom Steed's ETB requires another creature you control to exile, and with no board presence, its key synergy is wasted. Playing a land first and casting a cheaper creature like Merfolk Looter would develop the board more efficiently.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Phantom Steed ({3}{U}) before playing a land, with no other creatures on the battlefield.
annotations.betterLine: Play Choked Estuary (revealing Swamp to enter untapped), then cast Merfolk Looter ({1}{U}) to start filtering draws early.

annotations.description: On turn 1 with 3 mana available (likely), casting Rod of Absorption before playing a land is a sequencing error. The player should play their land first (Choked Estuary or Swamp) to ensure they have the mana available and don't miss a land drop. Additionally, Rod of Absorption on turn 1 is questionable - it's a slow value piece that does nothing immediately. Playing Choked Estuary (revealing a Swamp from hand) untapped and then casting the Rod would at least be correct sequencing if they wanted the Rod. However, with Obsessive Stitcher also available as a 3-drop that provides immediate card filtering, there's a reasonable argument the Stitcher is the better turn 1 play depending on the game plan.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Rod of Absorption without first playing a land.
annotations.betterLine: Play Choked Estuary (or Swamp) first, then decide between casting Rod of Absorption or Obsessive Stitcher. Playing land before spells is fundamental sequencing.

annotations.description: Casting Whims of the Fates before playing a land drop. The player has lands in hand (Jungle Hollow, Rakdos Carnarium, Swamp) and should play a land first before casting spells. Playing a land first is free and ensures the land isn't lost to Whims of the Fates' random pile sacrifice. Additionally, Whims of the Fates is a highly random card that can backfire, but the sequencing issue of casting spells before making a land drop is the clearest mistake here.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Whims of the Fates without first playing a land for the turn.
annotations.betterLine: Play a land first (likely Swamp for an untapped land, or Jungle Hollow for life gain), then decide whether to cast Whims of the Fates. Playing the land first ensures it enters the battlefield and can't be randomly sacrificed if it ends up in a chosen pile.

annotations.description: In Whims of the Fates, one of the three piles is randomly chosen to be sacrificed. The optimal strategy is to put all permanents into one pile and leave two piles empty, giving only a 1/3 chance of losing everything versus a guaranteed loss of whatever is in the chosen pile. By putting Consuming Aberration (a 32/32, their biggest threat and win condition) alone in one pile, there's a 1/3 chance of losing it for certain. If they had put all permanents in one pile, there would be a 1/3 chance of losing everything but a 2/3 chance of keeping everything intact. Isolating the best card in its own pile is strictly worse than grouping all permanents together.
annotations.actionTaken: Put Consuming Aberration alone in the first pile, apparently planning to spread permanents across multiple piles.
annotations.betterLine: Put all 16 permanents into a single pile and leave the other two piles empty. This gives a 2/3 chance of keeping everything and only a 1/3 chance of losing everything, which maximizes expected value.

annotations.description: In a pile-splitting effect, KimiK2 Sport put only Gamekeeper into the second pile while leaving a 32/32 Consuming Aberration, Yidris, Glint-Eye Nephilim, and all lands in the first pile. Their own reasoning stated they wanted to include 3 cards (Gamekeeper, Glint-Eye Nephilim, and an Island) but only selected Gamekeeper. This creates an extremely lopsided split that an opponent would exploit by giving them the tiny pile.
annotations.actionTaken: Selected only Gamekeeper for the second pile, creating a 15-to-1 split
annotations.betterLine: Should have created a more balanced split, or at minimum included the 3 cards mentioned in their reasoning (Gamekeeper, Glint-Eye Nephilim, Island) to make both piles somewhat viable

annotations.description: Playing Rakdos Carnarium as the first land on Turn 1 with no other lands in play forces the player to bounce the Carnarium itself back to hand (it's the only land they control when the ETB trigger resolves). This completely wastes the land drop, leaving the player with zero lands on the battlefield after Turn 1.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Rakdos Carnarium as their Turn 1 land drop with no other lands in play.
annotations.betterLine: Play Swamp for immediate untapped mana, or Dismal Backwater/Jungle Hollow which enter tapped but remain on the battlefield, ensuring a land is available for Turn 2.

annotations.description: Returning Command Tower to hand instead of a basic land is suboptimal. Command Tower is one of the best lands in Commander, producing any color of mana with no restrictions. A basic Forest would be redundant (there are 3 Forests available) and less valuable to bounce. By returning Command Tower, the player loses tempo on their best fixing land and will need to replay it tapped effectively wasting a land drop, whereas bouncing a basic Forest would preserve the superior mana base on board.
annotations.actionTaken: Returned Command Tower to hand from Rakdos Carnarium's ETB trigger.
annotations.betterLine: Return a basic Forest (having 3 on board, one is redundant) to preserve Command Tower's superior color fixing on the battlefield.

annotations.description: Command Tower is the best land in a 4-color Commander deck, providing all four colors of mana with no drawback. It enters untapped and taps for any color in your commander's identity. Discarding it is a significant loss because it cannot be easily recovered ('play again later' is incorrect - there's no inherent way to recur lands from the graveyard). The other options include taplands (Dismal Backwater, Jungle Hollow) or a basic Swamp, all of which are far less valuable than Command Tower. Alternatively, discarding a creature like Gamekeeper (which has a death trigger that could even benefit from being in the graveyard in some scenarios, though not directly) or a high-cost creature would be more appropriate.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Command Tower, the most versatile and valuable land in a multicolor Commander deck.
annotations.betterLine: Discard a tapland like Jungle Hollow or Dismal Backwater, or even the basic Swamp, as these are far less impactful than Command Tower in a 4-color deck that needs reliable color fixing.

annotations.description: Discarded the only land (Swamp) from a hand with just one land. annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Swamp, leaving the hand with zero lands.
annotations.betterLine: Discard a high-cost or color-mismatched card like Karmic Guide (requires white mana, costs 5) or Rod of Absorption (slower artifact), keeping the Swamp to have at least one land toward casting 2-drops like Merfolk Looter or Reassembling Skeleton.

annotations.actionTaken: Attempted to cast Sangromancer ({2}{B}{B}) on turn 1 with no lands in play.
annotations.betterLine: Play Jungle Hollow (or Dismal Backwater) as the land drop for turn 1, setting up mana for future turns.

annotations.actionTaken: Declined to play any land on turn 1, passing with both Dismal Backwater and Swamp in hand.
annotations.betterLine: Play Dismal Backwater on turn 1 (since it enters tapped, turn 1 is the least costly turn to play it), gaining 1 life and having it ready to produce mana on turn 2.

annotations.description: When forced to target one of their own creatures (likely with Bituminous Blast's 4 damage), KimiK2 Sport chose Horizon Chimera (a 3/2 with flash, flying, trample, and life-gain ability) instead of one of the 12 identical 2/2 Zombie Tokens. Horizon Chimera is a significantly more valuable creature with evasion and utility, while the Zombie Tokens are generic and expendable.
annotations.actionTaken: Targeted Horizon Chimera, destroying a creature with flying, trample, flash, and lifegain synergy.
annotations.betterLine: Target any one of the twelve 2/2 Zombie Tokens, preserving the much more valuable Horizon Chimera.

annotations.description: On turn 1 with no lands in play and 0 mana available, KimiK2 Sport attempted to cast Guiltfeeder, which costs {3}{B}{B} (5 mana). This is impossible without any mana sources. The player should have played a land first. They had both Dismal Backwater and Swamp available as land plays. The board shows hand=0 which is confusing, but the choices clearly include lands that should be played before any spells. Playing a land is the only legal and sensible turn 1 action here.
annotations.actionTaken: Attempted to cast Guiltfeeder ({3}{B}{B}) on turn 1 with no lands or mana available.
annotations.betterLine: Play Dismal Backwater (or Swamp) as the land for turn. Dismal Backwater is slightly better as it gains 1 life and provides color fixing, and since it enters tapped on turn 1 there's no tempo cost compared to later turns.

annotations.description: On turn 1 with only one land available (implied by the board state showing hand=0 after this choice, and the choices available), the player chose to cast Merfolk Looter which costs {1}{U} (2 mana) instead of playing a land first. Since it's turn 1, the player likely has only 1 land in play or needs to play their land drop first. More critically, they chose to cast Merfolk Looter over playing Plains as their land for the turn. Casting a 2-mana spell on turn 1 is impossible without acceleration, suggesting this is actually a selection/sequencing issue. The player should play their Plains first as their land drop, since they cannot cast Merfolk Looter (which requires {1}{U}) on turn 1 with just one land. Even if they somehow have mana available, playing the land before casting spells is correct sequencing to preserve information and maximize mana availability.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Merfolk Looter instead of playing Plains as their land drop first.
annotations.betterLine: Play Plains first as the land drop for the turn. The Merfolk Looter costs {1}{U} and cannot be cast on turn 1 without two lands including a blue source.

annotations.description: The player attempted to cast Obsessive Stitcher ({1}{U}{B}) but couldn't complete the mana payment, resulting in a rollback and wasted priority. On turn 1, the player likely only had one land available, making a 3-mana spell impossible to cast. The player should have known their available mana and chosen a castable spell or passed priority.
annotations.actionTaken: Attempted to cast Obsessive Stitcher (3 mana) on turn 1 with insufficient mana, resulting in a rollback.
annotations.betterLine: Pass priority or cast a spell within the available mana budget. With only 1 land on turn 1, no 3-mana spells are castable.

annotations.description: With a massive board of Sangromancer (3/3), 13 Zombie tokens (2/2 each), and Guiltfeeder (0/4), the player appears to have attacked with only Guiltfeeder (a 0/4 creature) instead of the entire board. Against an opponent at 40 life, the full board attacks for 29 damage. Attacking with just Guiltfeeder deals 0 combat damage plus graveyard-count life loss only if unblocked. The reasoning hallucinated that the opponent was at 2 life when they were at 40.
annotations.actionTaken: Attacked with only Guiltfeeder (0/4 with Fear) instead of the full board.
annotations.betterLine: Attack with all creatures ('All attack') to deal 29 damage and pressure the opponent significantly, or at minimum attack with all creatures that can safely attack.
